theme: Zophar’s rebuke; Job answers, I have heard all this before
readingInstruction: Read Job 11:1-13:28. Zophar, the third friend, speaks in chapter 11. Job’s reply fills chapters 12 to 14, but you will read the first part today, ending at chapter 13. As you read, mark every place where Job turns from his friends to speak to God.
settingTheScene: Now all three friends have spoken once. Eliphaz argued from experience and Bildad argued from tradition. Zophar is the sharpest of the three, and he argues from sheer confidence. He tells Job that he knows what God is thinking. Job’s answer begins with sarcasm and ends with one of the most daring statements of faith in the Bible. He will not give up on God, and he will not give up on the truth, and he is willing to say so to God’s face.
observation: Zophar asks, “Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right?” (11:2).
He wishes that God would speak and tell Job “that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves” (11:6).
He asks, “Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?” (11:7).
He promises that if Job repents, “you will forget your misery” and “your life will be brighter than the noonday” (11:13-17).
Job answers with sarcasm: “No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you” (12:2).
Job says, “I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you” (12:3). He says he has become a laughingstock to his friends.
He describes God’s power over nations and rulers: “He makes nations great, and he destroys them” (12:23).
He calls the friends “worthless physicians” and “whitewashers” who lie on God’s behalf (13:4, 7).
Job says, “Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face” (13:15).
He asks, “Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?” (13:24).
interpretation:
Zophar’s speech is a good example of a sound idea turned into a weapon. His question in 11:7 is a good one. No one can fully search out God. But he uses it against Job in the wrong way. He says that God’s wisdom is so deep that Job cannot possibly know that he is innocent. That is a remarkable thing to say to a man who has lost his children. If God is that deep, then Zophar should be more careful about telling Job what God is doing.

Job’s sarcasm in chapter 12 is earned. “Wisdom will die with you.” He tells them that he knows everything they have said. The wise sayings about God’s power and justice are not secret. Everyone knows them. The problem is not information. The problem is that they use these truths to hurt him. And then he does what none of them has done: he describes God’s power honestly. God overthrows the mighty and strips kings of their robes (12:17-21). God is a God who is not predictable, and the friends’ tidy picture of divine justice cannot contain him.

Then comes chapter 13, and the most famous line in this section. “Though he slay me, I will hope in him.” The ESV translation reflects one reading of the Hebrew. Some translations read it as “Behold, he will slay me; I have no hope.” Either way, the verse is full of tension, and the next clause is clear: “yet I will argue my ways to his face.” Job is not giving up on God. He is going to bring his case before God directly. He knows that the godless cannot approach God, and the fact that he is willing to do so is itself evidence of his faith (13:16).

Look at the difference between Job and the friends. The friends talk about God. Job wants to talk to God. They defend God, as though he needed it. Job asks for an audience. He is the one who takes God seriously, and so he is the one who is willing to be honest with him.

This is a kind of faith that asks questions and keeps coming back. It is not a faith that is afraid of the answer.
connection: The picture of faith that hopes in God even when he seems to be an enemy shows up again in Abraham, who believed that God could raise Isaac from the dead (Hebrews 11:17-19), and in Jesus in Gethsemane: “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Habakkuk 3:17-19 is another echo.
application:
Think of one question you are afraid to ask God. Ask it this week, honestly and respectfully, in prayer. Then keep listening.

Be careful of the kind of confidence that Zophar has. If you ever find yourself certain about why someone else is suffering, that is a sign to stop talking.

Consider memorizing Job 13:15 as your own statement of faith.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you do not understand about what he is doing.
Ask him to give you honesty in prayer and humility to wait.
Ask him to keep you hoping in him.
